title: Same push, twice the mass
hook: The same steady push, on a cart twice as heavy. What happens to its speed?

knows: heavier things are harder to push
that a newton (N) is a unit of force
doesNotKnow: that a constant force gives a steadily rising speed

misconception: A steady force gives a steady speed, and mass has little to do with how fast the speed changes.
objective: The learner can explain that a steady net force makes speed climb steadily, at a rate equal to force divided by mass, so twice the mass gains speed half as fast.

claims.text: Acceleration is force divided by mass (Newton's second law, a = F / m).
claims.source: Newton, Principia (1687), Law II; Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 5.

claims.text: A steady 10 N push on a 2 kg cart from rest gives 10 m/s after 2 s; on a 4 kg cart it gives 5 m/s, gaining 2.5 m/s every second.
A steady push does not give a steady speed: from rest, speed climbs in proportion to time, v = a t, for as long as the push lasts.
claims.source: Constant F gives constant a; integrating dv/dt = a from v = 0 gives v = a t. Halliday, Resnick and Walker, ch. 2 (constant acceleration).

claims.text: A bigger push makes speed climb faster: acceleration is proportional to the push (a = F / m), so doubling the push doubles the rate.
claims.source: a = F / m is proportional to F at fixed m. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 19): Derivation: a = F/m at fixed m is linear in F, so 2F gives 2a; from rest v = at, so the speed-time line is twice as steep. The reveal says 'a bigger push made the line steeper ... grows with the push', consistent.

claims.text: The track is frictionless and the push is constant; with friction, the net force would be the push minus friction.
claims.source: Stated idealisation; F in a = F / m is the net force (Halliday, Resnick and Walker, ch. 5).

recall.question: The same engine force pushes an empty van and the same van fully loaded to three times its mass. Ignoring friction, how does the loaded van's acceleration compare?
recall.why: Acceleration is force divided by mass: the same force on three times the mass gives one third the acceleration.
